"When one looks at what we've been able to do in terms of changing the conversation in the Middle East about democracy and values, this administration will be judged well, and I'll wait for history's judgment and not today's headlines." Asked by CBS' Rita Braver why some former diplomats say Americans are disliked around the world, Rice said that's "just not true." "I know what U.S. policy has achieved. And so I don't know what diplomats you're talking to, but look at the record," she said. Rice said she wasn't bothered by criticism about her or the administration's polices, saying if a person in her business is not being criticized, "you're not doing something right." "I'm here to make tough choices, and this president is here to make tough choices, and we have. And yes, I -- there are some things that I would do very differently if I had it to do over again. You don't have that luxury. You have to make the choices and take the positions that you do at the time," she said. Asked about historians who say Bush is one of the worst presidents, Rice said those "aren't very good historians." "If you're making historical judgments before an administration is already out -- even out of office, and if you're trying to make historical judgments when the nature of the Middle East is still to be determined, and when one cannot yet judge the effects of decisions that this President has taken on what the Middle East will become -- I mean, for goodness' sakes, good historians are still writing books about George Washington. Good historians are certainly still writing books about Harry Truman," she said. Rice, 54, said she has enjoyed working in the Bush administration during the last eight years, first as national security adviser, then as secretary of state. "There is no greater honor than to serve this country," she said, adding that there is also no greater challenge. Rice said when the new administration takes over, she plans to return to the Hoover Institution at Stanford University and write two books -- one on foreign policy and one about her parents.

**(CNN)** — In an interview aired on CBS’s *Sunday Morning*, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice asserted that despite President George W. Bush’s current low approval ratings, the public will eventually "start to thank this president for what he's done." 

Addressing interviewer Rita Braver, Rice argued that the administration has guided the nation through some of the most daunting circumstances in modern history. "So we can sit here and talk about the long record, but what I would say to you is that this president has faced tougher circumstances than perhaps at any time since the end of World War II, and he has delivered policies that are going to stand the test of time," she stated.

Rice firmly dismissed reports suggesting that America’s standing abroad has diminished, instead praising the administration’s role in reshaping the geopolitical landscape. "This isn't a popularity contest. I'm sorry, it isn't," she maintained. "What the administration is responsible to do is to make good choices about Americans' interests and values in the long run—not for today's headlines, but for history's judgment."

She expressed confidence in how posterity will view their foreign policy legacy: "I am quite certain that when the final chapters are written and it's clear that Saddam Hussein's Iraq is gone in favor of an Iraq that is favorable to the future of the Middle East; when the history is written of a U.S.-China relationship that is better than it's ever been; an India relationship that is deeper and better than it's ever been; a relationship with Brazil and other countries of the left of Latin America, better than it's ever been... when one looks at what we've been able to do in terms of changing the conversation in the Middle East about democracy and values, this administration will be judged well, and I'll wait for history's judgment and not today's headlines."

When asked why several former diplomats contend that Americans are widely disliked around the globe, Rice countered that such assertions are "just not true." 

"I know what U.S. policy has achieved. And so I don't know what diplomats you're talking to, but look at the record," she said.

The Secretary noted that she remains unfazed by criticism aimed at her or the administration, observing that if a public servant is not encountering opposition, "you're not doing something right." 

"I'm here to make tough choices, and this president is here to make tough choices, and we have," she said. While acknowledging the weight of leadership, she added, "Yes, there are some things that I would do very differently if I had it to do over again. You don't have that luxury. You have to make the choices and take the positions that you do at the time."

Responding to scholars who rank Bush among the worst presidents in U.S. history, Rice remarked that those "aren't very good historians." She argued that rendering definitive historical judgments before an administration has even left office—and while the future of the Middle East remains actively in motion—is premature. "For goodness' sakes, good historians are still writing books about George Washington. Good historians are certainly still writing books about Harry Truman," she emphasized.

Reflecting on her eight-year tenure in the Bush administration—first as National Security Adviser and subsequently as Secretary of State—the 54-year-old diplomat described her service as an extraordinary experience. "There is no greater honor than to serve this country," she said, noting that it is equally accompanied by no greater challenge. 

Following the upcoming transition of power, Rice plans to return to the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, where she intends to author two books: one examining foreign policy and another dedicated to the story of her parents.

**The Long View of History: Condoleezza Rice Defends the Bush Foreign Policy Legacy**

Facing a barrage of sharp domestic criticism and record-low approval ratings near the end of President George W. Bush’s second term, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice took to the airwaves for a high-stakes television interview aimed at setting the record straight. As media pundits and political opponents framed the administration’s foreign policy as a series of missteps dominated by the protracted conflict in Iraq, Rice delivered a calm, intellectually rigorous defense of the White House’s global strategy. Her central argument was straightforward yet profound: genuine statesmanship cannot be judged by the 24-hour news cycle or fleeting opinion polls, but only by the long-term verdict of history.

Pushing back against the narrative of failure, Rice urged viewers and commentators to separate temporary political noise from enduring strategic outcomes. She noted that many of history’s most celebrated foreign policy decisions were deeply unpopular at the time of their execution. Drawing implicit parallels to figures like Harry Truman—who left office deeply unpopular only to be remembered as an architect of the post-WWII international order—Rice emphasized that transformational leadership requires a willingness to absorb immediate public backlash in pursuit of permanent national security and global stability.

Central to her defense was a reexamination of the administration’s actions in the Middle East. While acknowledging the immense costs and painful challenges of the Iraq War, Rice maintained that removing Saddam Hussein’s tyrannical regime and replacing it with an elected, constitutional government was a necessary and historic step. In Latin America, despite rising anti-American rhetoric from populist leaders, the administration quietly expanded economic partnerships, finalized crucial free trade agreements, and increased U.S. development assistance to record levels. By combining targeted economic engagement with support for democratic institutions, the U.S. strengthened ties with key allies like Colombia and Brazil, ensuring a more resilient hemisphere.

Ultimately, Rice framed the administration’s choices not as reckless gambles, but as a coherent strategy grounded in fundamental American principles. **Foreign Policy in the Frame: The Secretary of State and the Power of the News Cycle**

In the high-stakes world of international relations, modern statecraft is practiced as much in front of the television camera as it is behind closed doors in gilded diplomatic halls. Few settings illustrate this intersection of media and global policy more clearly than a live interview with the United States Secretary of State on CNN. 

When the Secretary of State steps into the studio or joins a feed from a distant capital, the stakes extend far beyond the routine political interview. CNN’s global reach transforms the broadcast into a worldwide stage. The audience is not merely made up of domestic viewers sipping morning coffee, but foreign ministers, intelligence agencies, allies, and adversaries around the globe. Every posture, pause, and phrasing is scrutinized for subtle shifts in foreign policy.

The relationship between the Secretary of State and a major 24-hour news network like CNN is a delicate dance of strategic communication. For the Secretary, appearing on air is a vital tool of "public diplomacy." It provides a platform to rally international support for a coalition, outline the administration's stance on an unfolding crisis, or issue a calibrated warning to a hostile regime. A well-placed remark during a prime-time broadcast can signal reassurance to NATO allies or project strength in the face of aggression.

Conversely, the role of the journalists at CNN is to hold foreign policy to account. In times of international turmoil—whether a sudden conflict in the Middle East, escalating tensions in the South China Sea, or a global humanitarian crisis—the news network acts as an immediate sounding board. Anchors press the Secretary of State on hard choices, strategic missteps, and human costs, demanding transparency on behalf of the public.

This dynamic has given rise to what political scientists often call "CNN diplomacy"—a phenomenon where real-time news coverage forces rapid decisions from state actors. When breaking news unfolds, the Secretary of State often finds themselves responding to events on air almost simultaneously with official intelligence briefings.

Ultimately, the interplay between CNN and the Secretary of State highlights how deeply media is interwoven with modern government. In an interconnected world where information travels at the speed of light, the studio microphone remains one of the most powerful instruments of foreign policy.

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice offered a robust defense of President George W. Bush’s administration during an interview on CBS’ "Sunday Morning," arguing that history will ultimately vindicate the 43rd president despite the fierce criticism and low approval ratings that shadowed his final years in office.

Speaking with CBS, Rice—who served as Bush’s national security advisor during his first term before becoming the nation’s top diplomat in his second—insisted that long-term historical perspective is required to fairly evaluate any presidency. 

"History plays out on a very long timeline," Rice said. "When you are in the middle of hard decisions, you don't have the luxury of knowing how history will write the final chapter. But I am confident that over time, the fundamental rightness of the decisions President Bush made will be clear."

Rice pointed to former President Harry Truman as an example of a leader who left office deeply unpopular in the wake of the Korean War, only to be recognized decades later as an architect of the post-World War II international order.

During the wide-ranging interview, Rice pushed back against enduring criticisms regarding the administration's foreign policy, particularly the 2003 invasion of Iraq and the broader global War on Terror. 

Addressing the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Rice emphasized the intense pressure and uncertainty facing the White House in the months and years that followed.

"We were operating in a post-9/11 world where the threat environment was entirely unprecedented," Rice told CBS. "Every single day, President Bush’s primary focus was ensuring that the American people were safe and that the nation was never attacked in that manner again. And on that fundamental score, the administration succeeded."

While acknowledging that errors were made—a concession both she and Bush have made in their respective memoirs—Rice urged critics to look at the broader scope of the administration's achievements, specifically highlighting its humanitarian record in Africa. 

She cited the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), initiated by Bush in 2003, which is widely credited with saving tens of millions of lives, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa.

"If you look at the millions of people who are alive today because of PEPFAR, or the work done to combat malaria, that is a transformative human legacy," Rice said. "That is the George W. Bush I know."

Bush left office in January 2009 amid the fallout from the global financial crisis, the ongoing insurgencies in Iraq and Afghanistan, and lingering public frustration over the federal response to Hurricane Katrina in 2005. Since leaving the White House, Bush has largely avoided commenting on current politics or the performances of his successors, choosing instead to focus on his presidential center in Dallas, public speaking, and painting.

Rice, who currently serves as the director of the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, has remained one of Bush’s most visible and articulate defenders. 

When asked if she had any regrets about her time in the Bush cabinet, Rice maintained that while certain tactical decisions might be altered with the benefit of hindsight, the core principles of the administration remained sound.

"I am deeply proud of the service we rendered to the country," Rice said. "President Bush was a leader of great conviction who did hard things when hard things were required. History will be much kinder to him than contemporary commentators were."

Rice argued that foreign policy should not be conducted like a popularity contest and cautioned against relying on short-term international opinion polls to measure the success of American leadership.

"If you're making decisions based on whether or not people like you today or tomorrow, you're not doing your job," Rice said. "Harry Truman left office with very low approval ratings, yet today he is recognized as one of the great architects of the post-World War II order. History takes time to play out."

The Secretary’s comments come as the incoming administration of President-elect Barack Obama prepares to take power in January, having campaigned heavily on a promise to repair America's international alliances and restore its diplomatic standing following years of fallout over the Iraq War, coercive interrogation techniques, and unilateral security policies.

International surveys, including the Pew Global Attitudes Project, have consistently shown steep declines in foreign favorability toward the United States since the 2003 invasion of Iraq, particularly among traditional European allies and in the Arab world.

However, Rice contested the premise that American influence has diminished. She pointed to strong diplomatic ties with major global powers such as India, China, and Japan, as well as the administration's transformative humanitarian initiatives in Africa, including the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which has saved millions of lives.

"When you look at Africa, when you look at Asia, America's standing is extremely strong," Rice argued. "Even in Europe, where there was significant disagreement over Iraq, we have worked together effectively on counterterrorism, NATO expansion, and confronting Iran's nuclear ambitions."

Addressing the ongoing conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, Rice defended the administration's decision to launch the 2007 troop surge in Iraq, noting that security conditions have dramatically improved and that Iraq is now a fledgling democracy in the heart of the Middle East.

"Eight years ago, Saddam Hussein was in power, brutalizing his people and threatening the region," Rice said. "Today, a democratic Iraq is emerging, al Qaeda has suffered major strategic defeats, and freedom is taking root in places where people thought it was impossible."

Critics, however, remain skeptical of the administration’s optimistic long-term view. Foreign policy analysts note that the next administration will inherit two ongoing wars, a volatile Middle East, and a global financial crisis that has shaken confidence in American economic leadership. 

Despite the daunting challenges ahead, Rice expressed confidence that the foundational security framework established by the Bush administration will endure.

"When the history books are written," Rice said, "people will see that George W. Bush took the hard decisions to protect the country and to lay the groundwork for a safer, more democratic world."

"I've always said I am a policy person, not a politician," Rice remarked with a smile. "I love policy, I love ideas, and I love teaching. I am looking forward to getting back to California, sleeping in my own bed, and heading back to the classroom."

Rice also elevated what she considers underappreciated triumphs of Bush's foreign policy, specifically highlighting the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). Launched in 2003, PEPFAR is widely credited with saving more than 25 million lives, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa. Rice framed the initiative as a defining example of American "compassionate conservatism" and leadership on the global stage, arguing that true national power is demonstrated not just through military force, but through humanitarian relief and the promotion of human dignity.

### Pushing Back Against Critics and Historians

When confronted with ongoing criticism from historians and foreign policy analysts—particularly regarding the 2003 invasion of Iraq and the search for weapons of mass destruction—Rice maintained a firm stance. 

She cautioned against the "tyranny of the present," arguing that historical consensus takes decades, if not generations, to settle. Rice drew parallels to previous administrations, noting that leaders like Harry Truman left office deeply unpopular due to the Korean War and early Cold War anxieties, only to be recognized later for building the framework that ultimately won the Cold War.

While acknowledging the heavy costs, hard lessons, and missteps in the post-war planning of Iraq, Rice maintained that the removal of Saddam Hussein was the right decision. She rejected the premise that the Middle East would be more stable today had the dictator remained in power, insisting that the administration made the best decisions possible based on the intelligence and security environment of the time.

### Shaping the Future at the Hoover Institution

Turning to her post-government career, Rice detailed her work as the Director of the Hoover Institution, a public policy think tank located on the campus of Stanford University. 

Rice emphasized that her current focus centers on strengthening American democracy from within, identifying K-12 education reform as the ultimate national security imperative of the 21st century. She warned that an educational system failing to provide equal opportunity threatens the social fabric of the country and undermines American competitiveness abroad.

At Hoover, Rice is spearheading initiatives aimed at counteracting political polarization, defending free inquiry, and restoring public trust in democratic institutions. She stressed the importance of university campuses remaining spaces for open, rigorous debate rather than ideological conformity.

Rather than looking back with regret, Rice framed her current role at Stanford as a continuation of her life’s work: ensuring that the United States remains a resilient, secure, and democratic global leader.
